findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are canceled when the request ends
findings.body:
Each background goroutine (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) builds its timeout with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context.

The k8s handlers wrap that context in `context.WithTimeout` and `defer cancel()` it. net/http also cancels the request context as soon as ServeHTTP returns. So once the dual writer returns the storage result, the parent context is canceled almost immediately. The legacy write then races against that cancellation and will often fail with `context canceled`, which leaves legacy storage permanently out of sync.

The 10s timeout adds nothing, because the parent is canceled first. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent: it keeps request values such as the user identity but drops the cancellation.

findings.title: Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy metric
findings.body:
When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

As a result, storage create errors are reported as legacy-store errors and never show up in the storage error metric. That makes the dual-writer dashboards and alerts misleading.

findings.title: Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy metric
findings.body:
When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. The failure should go to `recordStorageDuration`.

Storage update errors are therefore misattributed to legacy storage and missing from the storage metrics.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded via recordStorageDuration
findings.body:
Inside the async goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the outcome is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`.

Legacy delete-collection latency and errors are counted as storage metrics. This pollutes the storage series and hides legacy failures.

findings.title: Object name passed as the `kind` metric label
findings.body:
On successful storage delete the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. It passes the object `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`.

This mislabels the metric. It also creates a new Prometheus label value for every deleted object name, which is unbounded label cardinality and can blow up memory and storage in the metrics backend.

findings.title: Legacy update re-applies the raw objInfo instead of the object written to storage
findings.body:
The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper` so legacy received exactly the object persisted in unified storage. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in a background goroutine.

The legacy store then calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own copy of the old object. For PATCH and server-side apply, the patch is applied to legacy's possibly different state, so the two stores can diverge. The patcher's transformers (patch application, mutating admission) also run a second time, asynchronously, after the request has completed. Keep using `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` for the legacy write.

findings.title: Unordered fire-and-forget goroutines can apply legacy writes out of order
findings.body:
Every write spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write, with no ordering or serialization.

Take a create or update followed quickly by a delete of the same object. The legacy Delete goroutine can run before the earlier Create/Update goroutine finishes. Legacy then ends up with a resurrected or stale object even though unified storage is correct. Because mode 3 never reads from legacy, the divergence goes unnoticed until a rollback to a lower mode. There is also no bound on the number of in-flight goroutines, and `Destroy` does not wait for them.

findings.title: Legacy write errors are silently dropped (no logging)
findings.body:
In all four async goroutines the legacy error only sets a boolean on a metric; it is never logged. The previous implementation logged legacy failures together with the object.

If legacy writes fail (for example from the context cancellation issue, validation, or conflicts), operators get no error message, object name, or cause to diagnose the divergence. Log `errObjectSt` / `err` with the request logger.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body:
`Delete` builds `log` with name/kind/method values but then calls `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`.

Downstream storage code that logs via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the name, kind and method fields. Every other method in this file passes `log`.

findings.title: Tests share one mock for both stores and never verify the async legacy write
findings.body:
Both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `mock.Mock`, so the tests cannot tell which store was called.

For example, the "error when creating object in the unified store fails" case only configures `setupLegacyFn`. It passes only because the storage Create call matches the expectation registered for legacy.

No test checks that:
- the legacy write is actually issued after a successful storage write,
- it is skipped when storage fails,
- Get and List never touch legacy.

The background goroutines also outlive the test. The core mode 3 behavior is effectively untested, which is how the canceled-context and metric bugs got through.

findings.title: Duplicate and unrelated go.work.sum entries
findings.body: The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, which is already present on the line above. It also adds a number of unrelated dependency checksums (azure sdk, alertmanager, older otel exporters). This is accidental churn from a local `go work sync` and should be dropped from a dual-writer change.
